title: The Two Faces of What You Are
reflection: Pick one worry-groove you know well. Next time your feet fall into it, notice the old path and take one small step off it: one breath, one softer word, one pause.

questions.q: Swamiji asks Kai whether he had to do anything to make the rain, a sensation or a thought known. What does Kai find, and what does it show?
o: Nothing: experience is already lit, and you never switch on the light of knowing.
Something: Kai had to turn his attention on first, so that each thing could become known to him.
Nothing: the rain, the sensation and the thought stayed hidden until he went and looked at them.
Only the rain: sounds are more obvious than the thoughts and the sensations in the body are.
questions.e: Kai says they are already lit and he did not do anything. As long as you are awake, experience is lit from within and the awareness you could not catch as an object is not a blank: it shines. This is Prakāśa, light, that which reveals.
questions.c: Awareness is already on: you never switch it on

questions.q: What does the image of the sun in a room show about awareness?
o: The sun lights everything and also itself, with no second sun: awareness reveals and is self-revealing.
The sun is far away, so awareness is far from us and can be reached only by long practice.
The sun rises and sets, so awareness comes and goes as a person wakes and falls asleep.
The sun needs a torch to be seen, so awareness needs a second awareness to notice the first.
questions.e: James says you do not shine a torch at the sun to see it. Likewise a thought needs no second awareness to notice it: awareness reveals the thought and in the same act reveals its own being-aware.
questions.c: Self-revealing: no second sun is needed

questions.q: Sarah rests in the bare fact of being present, without her name or worries, and finds it is “not blank.” What does she find, and what is it called?
o: A quiet hum of being here, alert and awake: living self-presence, called Vimarśa.
A silence with nothing in it, awake to nothing at all: the empty stillness called Prakāśa.
A thought about being present, repeated quietly: the habit of attention called Śakti.
A sensation in the body, felt at the chest: the bodily warmth that is called Vimarśa.
questions.e: Awareness is not just a light that reveals things; it is alive and knows itself as present. Swamiji says Prakāśa is the light and Vimarśa is the one who lives in the light and knows it.

questions.q: A friend says awareness is just like a mirror, a screen or a camera, since each of them takes in what is in front of it. What does the lesson reply?
o: They record, but none knows it does: no one is home, while awareness knows itself.
They are all alive in their own way, so awareness is just one more kind of mirror, screen or camera.
They are better than awareness, since they never forget anything that they have been shown or recorded.
Those are unrelated to awareness, so nothing can be learnt by comparing the two of them at all.
questions.e: Swamiji asks whether the mirror knows it reflects, whether the screen experiences the film, whether the camera enjoys the wedding. No: there is no one home. Awareness reveals like a mirror but also knows itself as present.
questions.c: A mirror, screen or camera has no one home

questions.q: Kai asks why embodied cognition matters, since the active brain seems obvious. What do the two examples in the lesson show?
o: A melody stirs a musician’s movement regions and “sandpaper” stirs touch: the brain reaches out to meaning.
A melody quietens the brain and the word “sandpaper” does nothing at all: the brain waits to be told what things mean.
Musicians have more active brains than other people do, so only a trained person can be said to be aware of things.
Words are stored in one region and sounds in another region, so the brain is a filing system for what it hears.
questions.e: The old picture was a passive machine, with meaning bolted on afterwards. Swamiji says meaning is built into perception from the first instant: the brain anticipates, simulates and participates. The contemplatives named this living quality Vimarśa roughly a thousand years earlier, a striking handshake but not a proof of one by the other.
questions.c: Embodied cognition: the brain reaches out

questions.q: “Prakāśa and Vimarśa are two separate properties that happen to come together, so one could in principle be had without the other.”
questions.e: Take away self-presence and you have a machine, like a security light; take away the light and you have a blank point present to nothing. Neither survives alone. Like the brightness and warmth of one flame, they are one awareness, which the course names Consciousness-Energy.
questions.c: The two faces cannot be separated

questions.q: “The course teaches that the ground of a person is a still, blank witness, and the world is only an illusion playing on an empty screen.”
questions.e: Swamiji calls this a common misreading and says the course says the opposite: the ground of you is not a blank screen; it is alive and creative, as in the quiet hum of being here Sarah noticed.
questions.c: The ground is alive, not a blank screen

questions.q: Kai feels that his bad patterns are permanent deposits sitting in the system. How does Swamiji answer?
o: The mind is alive: the patterns are processes it keeps going, so the same power can build differently.
The mind is a recorder, so the patterns are permanent and the only choice is to learn to live with them for good.
The mind is a machine, so the patterns can be changed only by a doctor, with outside help and some form of medicine.
The mind is a blank, so the patterns are not real and need no attention from anyone and no change of any kind.
questions.e: Swamiji offers two pictures: the mind as a recorder, with suffering as a deposit, and the mind as alive and self-modifying. The second is the true one. Neuroplasticity is mainstream science: the wiring changes with habitual use.

questions.q: Sarah says, “When I spiral into worry, I am training the worry.” What does Swamiji add?
o: Gently, yes, but if worry can be trained, so can steadiness, like a new path on a hillside.
Yes, and it cannot be undone, since a worn groove becomes a canyon carved in solid stone over the years.
No, since worry is only a feeling and has no effect at all on the way the brain is wired in the end.
No, since the circuits of the brain are fixed in childhood and cannot be changed in any adult at all.
questions.e: A groove is not a canyon carved in stone; it is just earth worn by repeated walking. Start walking a different line patiently, and a new path forms while the old one grows over. The patterns are not a verdict on who you are, just where you have been walking.
questions.c: A groove is worn earth, not stone

questions.q: In the practical experiment, what is Sarah asked to do when she feels her feet falling into her familiar worry-groove?
o: Notice “ah, the old path” without a fight, and take one small step off it: a breath, a softer word.
Fight the groove with all her strength, so that the whole hillside is flattened as soon as is possible.
Wait until the worry has passed, and only then think about it, since a pause is no use in mid-groove.
Ask her daughter to change her behaviour, so that the groove is no longer triggered at home again.
questions.e: Swamiji says she is not uprooting years in a day; she is starting a new line on the hill. James is asked to watch for the groove in his teaching, and Kai to try two minutes of steady attention on the breath daily, as an experiment and not a chore.
questions.c: One small step off the worn track
